figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Positioning of LoongSage relative to closely related systems. Each entry is compiled from the publicly available documentation of the corresponding project at the time of writing. A dash indicates a capability that is not documented, rather than one that cannot be realized within the system.
figures.headline: Comparison places LoongSage against related systems on four axes, with dashes marking capabilities that are not documented.
citing_sentences: Figure 1 situates LoongSage against the most closely related systems across four structural axes: training and inference backends, agent integration methodology, support for multi-teacher distillation, and execution asynchrony.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Overall system architecture of LoongSage.
figures.headline: Diagram shows AgentFlow governing the sampling plane, turning multi-turn agent interactions into trainable trajectories.
citing_sentences: As illustrated in Figure 2, the sampling plane is governed by AgentFlow, which translates unstructured multi-turn agent interactions into trainable trajectories.

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: The two orthogonal configuration axes behind LoongSage’s operational modes, their trade-offs, and the combination that the framework does not support.
figures.headline: Diagram shows placement and execution mode as orthogonal axes, with three of four combinations supported.
citing_sentences: Execution coupling and resource placement are treated as orthogonal architectural axes (Figure 3).

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: The AgentFlow request path. The Router intercepts each Chat Completions request, tokenizes the turn, dispatches it to SGLang’s /generate, and records the returned tokens per turn in the TrajectoryStore.
figures.headline: Request path shows the router tokenizing each chat turn, sending it to SGLang, and recording its tokens per turn.
citing_sentences: AgentFlow operates as the sampling plane enabling this abstraction—mediating among agents, the inference engine, and the training data pipeline to deterministically convert multi-turn interactions into replayable RL trajectories, as illustrated in Figure 4.

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: Data representation under TITO: a single flattened token array with its position-aligned response-space arrays, referenced by Segment and Triplet indices rather than copied.
figures.headline: Flattened token array with aligned arrays is referenced by index ranges rather than copied, so trajectory data is not duplicated.
citing_sentences: As depicted in Figure 5, AgentFlow represents each trajectory as a flattened, contiguous token array, tightly coupled with position-aligned arrays for loss masks, rollout log-probabilities, weight versions, routed experts, and token-level rewards.
Crucially, only mainline segments are designated as trainable, earning the right to populate the flat token, loss-mask, and log-probability arrays depicted in Figure 5.

figures.label: Figure 6
figures.caption: AgentFlow stores a black-box trajectory as a tree of segments: trainable mainline segments (origin=root or compact) own the flat token arrays, while a collab_spawn request forks a non-trainable subagent placeholder (origin=subagent).
figures.headline: Black-box trajectory is stored as a segment tree in which only root and compact mainline segments are trainable.
citing_sentences: To overcome this, AgentFlow records every trajectory as a directed tree of segments (Figure 6).

figures.label: Figure 7
figures.caption: The protocol adapter normalizes each agent’s wire format into one internal request: OpenCode over Chat Completions, Codex over OpenAI Responses, and Claude Code over Anthropic Messages. A single parser, tokenizer, and SGLang path then serve all of them.
figures.headline: Protocol adapters normalize OpenCode, Codex, and Claude Code formats into one shared parser, tokenizer, and inference path.
citing_sentences: Black-box agents utilizing proprietary APIs (i.e., those deviating from /v1/chat/completions) are bridged into the unified tree store via protocol adapters (Figure 7).

figures.label: Figure 8
figures.caption: The fully asynchronous pipeline’s control points reduce to two gates—a dispatch gate and a collection gate. Table 1 lists the mathematical bounds each registered policy places on them.
figures.headline: Asynchronous pipeline reduces to a dispatch gate and a collection gate, which each scheduling policy bounds.
citing_sentences: Figure 8 illustrates the resulting decoupled pipeline.
Because a scheduling strategy is entirely defined by the bounds it places on the two control gates (Figure 8), the surrounding controller logic remains invariant.

figures.label: Figure 9
figures.caption: The three registered sliding-window policies (a) no-window, (b) window-gated, and (c) windowed-fifo on a shared timeline of dispatched groups (bounds in Table 1, consequences discussed above).
figures.headline: Timelines show how no-window, window-gated, and windowed-fifo policies differ in dispatching groups under shared bounds.
citing_sentences: Table 1 formalizes the bounds of the three registered policies, visually mapped onto a shared timeline in Figure 9.
no-window (Figure 9a) dispatches a new group the moment an active slot frees up.
window-gated (Figure 9b) imposes a hard gate, refusing to dispatch any task whose sequence number exceeds the oldest in-flight one by more than the window $W=B(1+S)$.

figures.label: Figure 10
figures.caption: TransferMesh packs the named tensor stream into one contiguous memory bucket described by a single metadata frame, then dynamically selects a transport protocol per receiver based on device topology: utilizing a zero-copy CUDA IPC handle for colocated engines and an NCCL broadcast for remote receivers.
figures.headline: TransferMesh packs weights into one bucket and routes them over CUDA IPC for colocated engines and NCCL broadcast for remote ones.
citing_sentences: Figure 10 depicts this topology-aware routing architecture.

figures.label: Figure 11
figures.caption: The Teacher Manager schedules teacher groups that share a GPU-memory slot, offloading inactive teacher weights to host memory and swapping them back on demand.
figures.headline: Teacher Manager shares one GPU-memory slot among teacher groups, offloading inactive teacher weights to host memory.
citing_sentences: Figure 11 illustrates this resource pooling arrangement.

figures.label: Figure 12
figures.caption: Full-vocabulary distillation via micro-batch logit reconstruction: within each micro-batch the teacher logits are rebuilt from hidden states, consumed by the loss, and released before the next micro-batch begins.
figures.headline: Full-vocabulary distillation rebuilds teacher logits per micro-batch and releases them before the next micro-batch begins.
citing_sentences: Figure 12 illustrates this reconstruction architecture.

figures.label: Figure 13
figures.caption: Train–inference consistency is handled in three groups: source alignment guarantees the trained sequence mathematically matches the sampled sequence, long-context and precision settings anchor numerical stability, and residual corrections continuously bound the remaining gap.
figures.headline: Train–inference consistency is organized into source alignment, precision anchoring, and residual correction.
citing_sentences: To counteract this drift, the framework implements a defense-in-depth strategy categorized into source alignment, precision anchoring, and residual correction (summarized in Figure 13).

figures.label: Figure 14
figures.caption: Training curves for DeepSeek-V4-Flash on SWE tasks.
figures.headline: Entropy falls from approximately 0.24 to 0.21 while mean rollout reward stabilizes between 0.75 and 0.80.
citing_sentences: Figure 14 tracks DeepSeek-V4-Flash trained on complex SWE tasks.

figures.caption: Training curves for DeepSeek-V4-Flash on DAPO mathematical reasoning.
figures.headline: Mean rollout reward rises from roughly 0.45 to nearly 0.80 as step latency falls from 900 to 550 seconds.
citing_sentences: Figure 15 details DeepSeek-V4-Flash executing DAPO mathematical reasoning.

figures.caption: Training curves for full-vocabulary multi-teacher MOPD on Qwen3-30B-A3B.
figures.headline: Entropy rises from 0.31 toward 0.42 while step latency decreases from 1100 to 700 seconds.
citing_sentences: Figure 16 showcases full-vocabulary multi-teacher MOPD training for Qwen3-30B-A3B.

figures.caption: Training curves for Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B with the OpenCode black-box agent.
figures.headline: Black-box OpenCode run shows mean rollout reward climbing from 0.35 to 0.50 while end-to-end time stays between 1500 and 2000 seconds.
citing_sentences: Figure 17 plots the Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B training utilizing the opaque OpenCode black-box agent, heavily reliant on real code operations and multi-turn environments.

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a critical phase in the post-training pipeline of large language models (LLMs). As the frontier of LLM capabilities shifts from static reasoning to agentic tasks—characterized by external tool invocation, multi-turn interactions, and long-horizon decision-making—existing mainstream RL frameworks have grown increasingly unwieldy, raising the overhead of adoption, usage, and debugging. To address these challenges, we present LoongSage, an agent-native, fully asynchronous RL framework with a lightweight core of roughly 14K lines of code. Built upon Megatron for distributed training and SGLang for high-throughput inference, LoongSage centralizes orchestration within a single controller process and encapsulates all GPU-resident components as Ray actors. It introduces AgentFlow, a unified execution paradigm that orchestrates both white-box and black-box agents. For asynchronous execution, it integrates sliding-window strategies that bound trajectory staleness, and employs TransferMesh, a topology-aware synchronization mechanism that routes weights after each step over the fastest transport available to each receiver. Beyond agentic RL, LoongSage incorporates a memory-efficient Teacher Manager that decouples the scaling of teacher models from GPU memory constraints, natively supporting Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation. Extensive evaluations across four complete training runs, spanning complex reinforcement learning and multi-teacher distillation, demonstrate that task rewards improve steadily while the train–inference gap is kept under continuous control, and the fully asynchronous pipeline removes synchronous idle bubbles, sustaining hardware utilization.

sections.body: The paper argues that existing RL frameworks, built on single-turn RLHF and verifiable-reward assumptions, add production overhead for agentic training. It names three gaps: memory limits on the number of teachers, long-tailed rollouts that idle synchronous loops, and off-policy drift from tokenization, numerical precision, and MoE routing mismatches between training and inference. LoongSage is presented as a lightweight framework on Megatron and SGLang with six features: token-level agent integration through AgentFlow, staleness-bounded asynchronous training, topology-aware weight synchronization through TransferMesh, full-vocabulary multi-teacher distillation through a Teacher Manager, train–inference consistency mechanisms, and a configuration-driven plugin system. The authors also state that they open-source validated training recipes.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Existing RL frameworks add overhead for agentic training, so the paper proposes LoongSage, built on Megatron and SGLang.

sections.body: The related-work section places LoongSage among post-training methods and RL frameworks. It covers the move from RLHF to verifiable-reward training, agentic RL with multi-turn tool use, and distributed backends such as Megatron-LM, DeepSpeed, Ray, vLLM, and SGLang. It reviews frameworks including OpenRLHF, NeMo-Aligner, TRL, verl, and slime, and asynchronous systems including AReaL and Agent-Lightning. The authors argue that agentic workloads still need explicit support for trajectory structure, resource sharing, and the boundary between rollout and optimization. They conclude that a framework should expose the trade-off between utilization and staleness as a configurable policy rather than a fixed behavior.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Related work argues that existing RL frameworks lack explicit support for agentic trajectories, resource sharing, and rollout–optimization boundaries.

sections.body: Section 3 describes the architecture and its three design principles: one controller over Ray actors, token-level internal boundaries, and a thin trunk with named registry seams. Seven planes (control, sampling, training, algorithm, data, transfer, and resource) communicate through data objects and control interfaces. In default synchronous mode, a training step runs four stages: sampling, admission, aggregation, and update. Figure 3 is cited to show that execution coupling and resource placement are orthogonal axes, and that three of the four combinations are structurally supported. Fully asynchronous execution conflicts with colocated placement because both engines must stay resident in memory at once. This section reports no benchmark results.
sections.heading: The LoongSage Framework
sections.headline: The architecture uses one controller over Ray actors, token-level internal interfaces, and seven planes, with three of four placement combinations supported.

sections.body: Section 4 describes the mechanisms behind the feature list. AgentFlow exposes an OpenAI Chat Completions interface and stores each trajectory as one flat token array with aligned loss masks, log-probabilities, and weight versions, avoiding re-tokenization through Token-In, Token-Out. White-box agents produce linear trajectories, while black-box agents produce segment trees in which only mainline segments are trainable and subagent segments are placeholders. Asynchronous training bounds staleness with three sliding-window policies, each defined by dispatch and collection bounds in Table 1. TransferMesh selects a transport for each receiver, and the Teacher Manager offloads inactive teacher weights to host memory. Registries expose ten core extension points. The section gives no quantitative results.
sections.heading: Key Features
sections.headline: AgentFlow stores white-box and black-box agent trajectories as token arrays and segment trees, and three sliding-window policies bound asynchronous staleness.

sections.body: The evaluation reports four complete training runs: SWE and DAPO on DeepSeek-V4-Flash, OpenCode on Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B, and multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) on Qwen3-30B-A3B. Each metric traces one continuous run rather than an average over several trials. The tracked metrics are entropy, `rollout/reward_mean`, the approximate K3 KL gap, and step time. A separate asynchronous ablation on Qwen3-30B-A3B across two H20 nodes reports average step time of 580.79 s for the colocated baseline and 428.76 s for the best asynchronous configuration over 100 steps, a 1.35× speedup. Excluding step 0, the steady-state average is 414.58 s, a 1.40× speedup. The authors note that this ablation uses one workload where long-tail latency is severe enough for overlap to matter.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: Four training runs show rising rewards with bounded train–inference gaps, and asynchronous execution gives a 1.35× speedup.

sections.body: The conclusion restates LoongSage as a single-controller framework and lists six contributions: TITO integration for white-box and black-box agents, staleness-bounded asynchronous execution, TransferMesh weight synchronization, memory-multiplexed full-vocabulary multi-teacher distillation, train–inference consistency by design, and a zero-fork, configuration-driven plugin core. It states that the evaluations validate agentic training while strictly bounding train–inference divergence. The roadmap adds cross-node distributed storage for multi-teacher weights, native low-precision training primitives, PPO, SFT, LoRA, and omni-modal architectures. The conclusion does not discuss limitations, which the appendix covers.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: The conclusion lists six contributions and plans to add Proximal Policy Optimization, Supervised Fine-Tuning, and Low-Rank Adaptation.

sections.body: The appendix lists research and engineering authors in alphabetical order by first name. Appendix B reports infrastructure faults found while stabilizing the DeepSeek-V4-Flash SWE recipe. Hard failures include NaNs in early Megatron-Core versions with shared-expert overlap enabled, SGLang exhausting device VRAM during topology weight updates, and a CPU optimizer that exhausted host memory and crashed. Silent corruptions include a PDL dependency anomaly in a FlashInfer kernel that inflated the measured train–inference gap, and a parameter with identical shapes but different memory layouts across engines. The stated current boundaries are unfinished protocol adapters, ambiguous classification of compaction versus subtask branches, an interface-only cross-node teacher-weight cache, and an asynchronous mode that does not yet match the synchronous path's generality.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists author names and operational notes on hard failures, silent corruptions, and current implementation boundaries.
